Just because a treatment is trending doesn’t mean it’s the right treatment for you.

Sculptra has seen a significant rise in popularity, driven in part by the growing conversation around collagen stimulation and “regenerative” aesthetics.

But trends can oversimplify something that should always be highly individualized.

In aesthetic medicine, the question shouldn’t be “What treatment is everyone getting?” It should be “What is actually causing the change I’m trying to correct?”

Volume loss, skin laxity, texture, and structural changes are not the same—and they shouldn’t automatically be treated the same way.

In this video, Dr. Ostad shares his perspective on the rise of Sculptra, where it can have a role, and why choosing a treatment based on anatomy and long-term goals will always matter more than choosing one based on popularity.

Good aesthetic medicine isn’t about following trends. It’s about knowing when—and when not—to treat.

The neck is often one of the first areas to show visible signs of aging, yet it can be one of the most challenging areas to rejuvenate.

This before & after shows the results of Fraxel CO₂ laser resurfacing, with a noticeable softening of the deeper horizontal wrinkles, improved texture, and an overall smoother, more refined appearance to the skin.

CO₂ resurfacing works by creating controlled micro-injuries in the skin, initiating a natural healing response and stimulating the production and remodeling of collagen. What makes this result especially meaningful is the improvement in the depth and definition of the wrinkles. Rather than simply making the skin look temporarily smoother, the goal is to encourage structural remodeling within the skin for a more natural, gradual rejuvenation.

And collagen remodeling doesn’t stop when the skin has healed. The skin can continue to improve in the months following treatment as new collagen develops and reorganizes.

We often focus on rejuvenating the face, but the neck deserves the same attention. Treating the face and neck as a continuum can create a much more balanced and natural-looking result.

caption:
There has been a growing trend, particularly among plastic surgeons, of criticizing dermal filler and pointing to overfilled faces as evidence that patients should abandon injectables in favor of surgery.

I understand where some of that criticism comes from.

For years, aesthetic medicine went through an era where nearly every sign of aging seemed to have the same answer: add more volume. Cheeks, temples, jawlines, lips—every hollow became something to fill.

But when filler is repeatedly added without reassessing the patient's anatomy, it can create heaviness, distorted proportions and an unnatural appearance.

That’s a problem with how filler is being used—not filler itself.

As both a dermatologist and surgeon, I don’t see filler and surgery as opposing philosophies. They are different tools designed to accomplish different things.

A facelift can reposition descended tissue and address significant laxity in a way filler cannot. But strategically placed filler can restore support, improve proportion and subtly balance the face without surgery.

The question shouldn’t be, “Filler or surgery?”

It should be, “What is actually causing the change we’re seeing?”

Sometimes the answer is filler. Sometimes it’s a laser or another technology. Sometimes it’s surgery. And sometimes, the right answer is to do nothing.

That’s also why I don’t believe in treating filler as a commodity.

Faces don’t come in syringes.

Every patient has different anatomy, volume loss, skin quality and goals. Treatment should follow the anatomy—not a predetermined number of syringes or a social media trend.

I welcome the conversation around overfilling. But swinging the pendulum from “filler for everything” to “filler is bad” is another oversimplification.

Natural-looking aesthetic medicine isn’t about filler vs. surgery.

It’s about having the judgment—and restraint—to know when to use each.

— Dr. Ariel Ostad

At our practice, we’ve long understood that true wellness begins beneath the surface—that the mind, body, and skin are deeply interconnected, and that stress and our overall state of wellbeing can influence how we look, feel, and function .

For more than two decades, Dr. Ostad has studied the powerful connection between the mind, stress, and skin health—how our mental and emotional state can influence certain skin conditions.

That understanding drives everything we do and is the reason we are excited to introduce Exomind™—an FDA-cleared transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) technology with a proven medical history, now entering the world of cognitive & mental wellness.

1. What is Exomind™?
Exomind™ is a non-invasive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) technology designed to influence neural activity in targeted areas of the brain. TMS has been studied and used in medicine for decades, and today this established technology is also being explored within the growing field of cognitive wellness.

2. What is TMS?
Transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, uses carefully controlled magnetic pulses to stimulate targeted areas of the brain. Unlike medication, TMS does not require anything to be injected or ingested, and the treatment is performed while you remain awake and comfortable.

3. Why are we offering Exomind?
Dr. Ostad has always viewed the skin as part of a larger system. Throughout his career, he has studied the relationship between the skin, stress, inflammation, sleep, and overall wellbeing.
We know that factors such as stress and sleep can influence a number of dermatologic conditions, including psoriasis, eczema, seborrheic dermatitis, acne, rosacea, and certain forms of hair shedding.
Exomind represents a natural extension of this philosophy—expanding our approach from caring for the skin and body to also supporting cognitive wellness and overall wellbeing.

caption:
Twenty-five years ago, on the morning of September 11th, I was performing Mohs surgery on a patient who was an NYPD officer.

We were in the middle of his procedure when news began to reach us about what was happening at the World Trade Center. I had removed the skin cancer, but I had not yet reconstructed the surgical defect on his nose.

Without hesitation, he got up from the chair.

With an open wound on his nose, his first thought wasn't about himself. He simply said:

“I have to go help my brothers.”

I have never forgotten that moment.

To me, it represents so much of what New York showed the world that day — extraordinary courage, selflessness, loyalty, and an instinct to help others when they needed it most.

Twenty-five years later, I still think about that officer and the countless first responders, healthcare workers, firefighters, police officers, volunteers, and everyday New Yorkers who put themselves aside to help someone else.

September 11th will always carry profound sadness. But it is also a reminder of the strength of this city and the character of the people who call it home.

I am incredibly proud to be a New Yorker, and it remains one of the greatest privileges of my career to care for and serve the brave, resilient people of this city.

Today, we remember those we lost, honor those who answered the call, and carry forward the strength and unity that defined New York in the days that followed.

We will never forget.

A new chapter in melanoma treatment is emerging.

Recent Phase 3 results surrounding a personalized mRNA melanoma vaccine have generated significant attention—and for good reason. But what does a “melanoma vaccine” actually mean?

In this video, Dr. Ostad explains what this new research means, why it matters, and why knowing your skin remains as important as ever.

Unlike a traditional vaccine, this investigational therapy is not designed to prevent someone from developing melanoma. Instead, it is created for certain patients who have already had a high-risk melanoma surgically removed, with the goal of helping the immune system recognize the cancer and reduce the risk of recurrence or spread.

It’s an exciting glimpse into the future of personalized medicine. But even as treatment advances, our most important tools remain the ones we have today: prevention and early detection.

Daily sun protection, regular skin examinations, and paying attention to new or changing spots can make an enormous difference—particularly because melanoma is highly treatable when detected early.
